newsitem.title: UK: Scandal-battered British royals debate future role.
newsitem.headline: Scandal-battered British royals debate future role.

text.p: Britain's royal family held an extraordinary summit on its future on Monday after embarrassing scandals plunged the once-venerated monarchy into disfavour.
A television opinion poll last month showed that 52 percent of viewers wanted to abolish the royalty before Prince Charles could become king.
The royals, known among themselves as "The Firm", sought to brush up an image tarnished by marital breakups and spending sprees by the younger generation.
Discussions ranged from how the family reputation can recover from dual divorces to how members will finance their luxury lifestyle, a frequent target of critical headlines.
Equal opportunities for princesses and the monarch's role as head of the official Church of England were also on the agenda, according to Britain's royalty-obsessed media.
Queen Elizabeth, her husband Prince Philip, sons Charles, Andrew and Edward and daughter Princess Anne joined the conference at the summer residence in Balmoral, Scotland, according to royal sources.
A spokeswoman at Buckingham Palace said it was one of a regular series of gatherings to plot the future of the family.
"There was a meeting with the prime minister (John Major) over the weekend," she said. "The royal family are having a meeting today." She gave no further details.

Respect for the 1,000-year-old monarchy is at an all-time low after the messy divorces this year of both heir to the throne Charles, from Princess Diana, and Andrew from the Duchess of York, the former Sarah Ferguson.
Irreverent newspapers speculate on royal sex lives while paparazzi scuffle for scandalous photographs of even "minor royals".

Many of the queen's subjects believe the ancient institution should take on a new mantle for the 21st century. Not only the succession but the monarch's role as Supreme Governor of the Church of England are seen as anachronistic.
According to media reports, which have proved accurate in the past, the family has split into two factions, with the older members wanting to hold on to as much tradition as possible.
But they say Prince Charles is leading a rebellion with calls for a more modern approach.

A possible change to laws of succession would let the eldest child, and not just the eldest son, become heir to the throne. Such an egalitarian attitude would bring Britain into line with other monarchies like Sweden and Norway.

Charles has indicated he would like to see a new approach to religion, styling himself "Defender of Faiths" rather than "Defender of the Faith" -- a title bestowed by the Pope on Henry VIII just before he broke away from Rome to establish the Church of England in the 16th century.
There has also been talk of ending a 300-year-old law that says anyone married to a Catholic cannot take the throne.

More urgent is the question of how to treat royal girlfriends. Charles has been parading longtime mistress Camilla Parker Bowles in the hope that she will be accepted by a British public who blame her for the break-up of Charles's marriage.

The future position of Diana, the most glamorous royal during her 15-year marriage, may also be discussed. She now operates as a semi-detached member of the royal family and wants some sort of role as an ambassador for Britain.
Then there is the question of money. The queen, one of the world's richest women, sought to counter criticism of her wealth by offering in 1992 to pay income tax for the first time.

The royal family may have pay their way even more, reducing the number of "royals" funded by the public purse, although newspapers said they would not return to the 18th century practice of living entirely off income from their huge estates.
